title: Finalizers versus Dispose (deterministic cleanup)
hook: Dispose releases resources when you call it — usually in a using block. A finalizer is a last-chance safety net the garbage collector runs later on a separate thread. For SkiaSharp bitmaps and file handles, Dispose is the right tool.

blocks.text: IDisposable.Dispose lets you release unmanaged resources deterministically — native handles, pooled connections, file streams. IAsyncDisposable does the same for async cleanup. A finalizer (~ClassName) runs when the garbage collector reclaims an object, on the finalizer thread, with no guaranteed timing. The dispose pattern combines both: Dispose does the work; a finalizer only as a backstop if someone forgets Dispose.

entries.plainDefinition: Explicit method to release resources immediately when you are done with an object.
entries.example: using var stream = File.OpenRead(path); // Dispose called at end of block

entries.plainDefinition: A method the runtime calls before reclaiming an object, on a dedicated thread.
Tells the runtime not to run the finalizer because Dispose already cleaned up.
entries.example: GC.SuppressFinalize(this) at the end of Dispose.

blocks.text: Native libraries like SkiaSharp hold unmanaged memory outside the managed heap. If you rely on finalizers, native memory stays allocated until a full garbage collection notices the wrapper is dead — possibly after thousands of requests. That looks like a memory leak in production. await using with IAsyncDisposable is the modern pattern for async pipelines that stream IAsyncEnumerable.

blocks.title: SkiaSharp rule
blocks.body: Wrap SKBitmap, SKSurface, and similar types in using or await using. Never assume the finalizer will run promptly.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: using block exits
items.body: Dispose runs synchronously on the current thread; native handle released now.

items.title: No Dispose called
items.body: Object becomes eligible for GC; finalizer is queued if one exists.

items.title: Finalizer thread runs
items.body: Runs later, one object at a time — unpredictable delay.

items.title: Object actually collected
items.body: Finalizable objects survive an extra GC cycle, extending lifetime.

diagram.title: Dispose vs finalizer timing
diagram.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant Dispose
  participant GC
  participant Finalizer
  App->>Dispose: using block ends
  Dispose-->>App: native freed now
  Note over App,GC: If no Dispose
  GC->>Finalizer: queue finalizer
  Finalizer-->>GC: late native cleanup

snippet.label: Standard dispose pattern
snippet.explanation: Dispose does real work. Finalizer is fallback. SuppressFinalize skips the finalizer when Dispose ran.

snippet.label: await using for async disposal
snippet.explanation: await using calls DisposeAsync at the end of the block — important for async I/O types.

snippet.label: SkiaSharp bitmap in using
snippet.explanation: SKBitmap wraps native pixels. using ensures immediate release instead of waiting for GC.

snippet.label: Spot native leak via dotnet-counters
snippet.code:
dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> \
  System.Runtime[gc-heap-size,gen-2-gc-count]
# Managed heap flat but process RSS grows → native leak; check Dispose
snippet.explanation: When managed heap is stable but process memory climbs, undisposed native wrappers (SkiaSharp, DB handles) are a prime suspect.

blocks.title: Resource cleanup models
rows: No IDisposable; rely on GC and explicit .destroy() on some APIs
Native addons use finalization or explicit close
WeakRef/finalization registry in modern JS — also delayed

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Relying on finalizers for SkiaSharp or database connections. Throwing from Dispose without guarding _disposed. Implementing a finalizer on every class — only types that wrap unmanaged resources need one.

blocks.text: Dispose is deterministic: runs synchronously (or via DisposeAsync) on the calling thread when using/await using exits. A finalizer (~Type) is queued when the object becomes unreachable; the finalizer thread runs it later with no timing guarantee. Finalizable objects survive one extra GC cycle because they are resurrected onto the finalizer queue. GC.SuppressFinalize(this) in Dispose skips that cycle. How to prove it in production: dotnet-counters shows gc-heap-size stable but process RSS climbing — classic undisposed native wrapper pattern (SkiaSharp, sockets, file handles).

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Safety net for native interop wrappers only
Pure managed POCOs with no native handles

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'GC will clean up SkiaSharp bitmaps' or implementing finalizers on every class. Strong answer: Dispose is deterministic; finalizer is last-chance; finalizable objects cost an extra GC cycle.

interviewTakeaways: Dispose releases resources deterministically; finalizers run later on a dedicated thread with no timing guarantee.
Finalizable objects survive an extra GC cycle — only add a finalizer when wrapping unmanaged resources.
Wrap SkiaSharp, Npgsql, and file streams in using or await using; monitor RSS vs managed heap for native leaks.
60s: Dispose now on using exit. Finalizer is a delayed safety net on another thread. SuppressFinalize skips extra cycle. Native wrappers need Dispose.
Follow-up: when is IAsyncDisposable required over IDisposable?
commonPitfalls: Expecting finalizers to free SkiaSharp promptly — that gets you rejected because native memory stays until the finalizer thread runs.
Strong answer: using/await using for deterministic cleanup; finalizer only as backstop with SuppressFinalize.
Implementing finalizers on managed-only classes — adds GC overhead with no benefit.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node streams have .destroy(); Web Streams have abort. C# using is the idiomatic deterministic pattern for IDisposable.
JS FinalizationRegistry is also delayed and non-deterministic — like C# finalizers. Neither replaces explicit .destroy() or using for native resources.
